set_title: Fever, emboli or a mitral rumble: tumor, vegetation or rheumatic valve
stem: A 6-month-old girl has infantile spasms and hypopigmented patches on the trunk. Echocardiography shows multiple well-circumscribed masses in the ventricular walls. There is no fever and blood cultures are sterile.
oneliner: 6-month-old girl + infantile spasms + hypopigmented patches + multiple ventricular wall masses → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Myxoma is a **solitary atrial tumor in adults**
whyNot.A: Endocarditis needs **fever and positive cultures**; she has neither
whyNot.D: Rheumatic fever follows **strep pharyngitis in school-age children**
whyNot.E: Mitral stenosis is an **adult sequela** with a murmur, not ventricular masses

why: Tuberous sclerosis (TSC1 or TSC2) causes seizures, ash-leaf spots and **ventricular rhabdomyomas**, the most common fetal and infant cardiac tumor, which often regress spontaneously.

Systemic features

Diastolic rumble and **tumor plop that change with position**

**Gelatinous mass with stellate cells in myxoid stroma**
Damaged valve, IV drug use, prosthetic valve, dental procedure
Fever, Roth spots, splinter hemorrhages, Janeway lesions
**Opening snap then diastolic rumble** at the apex

set_title: High lipids: which pattern
stem: A 24-year-old man has an LDL cholesterol of 280 mg/dL and a triglyceride level of 120 mg/dL. His father had a myocardial infarction at age 45.
oneliner: 24M + LDL 280 + triglycerides 120 + father with MI at 45 → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Combined hyperlipidemia also **raises triglycerides**; his triglycerides are normal at 120 mg/dL
whyNot.B: Lipoprotein lipase deficiency gives **triglycerides above 1,000 mg/dL** in childhood; his are 120
whyNot.C: Hypertriglyceridemia has **raised triglycerides with normal LDL**; he has the reverse
whyNot.D: Dysbetalipoproteinemia raises **both cholesterol and triglycerides**; his triglycerides are normal

why: A defective LDL receptor leaves LDL in the blood, so LDL is very high from birth while **triglycerides stay normal**, and coronary disease comes early. Statins still work in heterozygotes because they increase LDL receptors made from the normal allele.

head: LDL
Triglycerides
Exam and family clue
First-line drug
rows: **Very high (190 mg/dL or more; above 500 in homozygotes)**
Tendon xanthomas, corneal arcus; autosomal dominant LDL receptor defect; early coronary disease
High-intensity statin; add ezetimibe or a PCSK9 inhibitor
Raised, or normal in some relatives
**Raised, with the pattern varying between relatives**
Early coronary disease; apoB overproduction; no tendon xanthomas
Statin; add a fibrate or omega-3 if triglycerides remain high
Pancreatitis risk, eruptive xanthomas; excess VLDL production
Fibrate (with lifestyle change and alcohol and sugar restriction)

idea.rule: Very high LDL with normal triglycerides and early coronary disease in the family = familial hypercholesterolemia.
also: Autosomal dominant LDL receptor defect; tendon xanthomas and corneal arcus are typical
Statins upregulate LDL receptors, so they work in heterozygotes
Homozygotes may need LDL apheresis

whyNot.C: **Age 40** fits both
whyNot.E: Both are usually **silent until a complication**

why: Cholesterol-rich LDL deposits in tendons, so **Achilles tendon xanthomas** point to familial hypercholesterolemia. In isolated hypertriglyceridemia LDL is normal and the skin findings, when present, are eruptive xanthomas.

set_title: Kidney or ureter formed wrong: fused, missing or blocked
stem: A 29-year-old primigravid woman has ultrasonography at 20 weeks that shows no right kidney. The sonographer cannot yet tell whether the left kidney is also absent.
oneliner: 29F + 20 weeks + no right kidney seen + left kidney unclear → ?
ask: Which single finding on the same scan would favor bilateral renal agenesis over unilateral renal agenesis?

options.A: An amniotic fluid index of 2 cm
options.E: No ectopic kidney in the pelvis

whyNot.B: The right kidney is already absent in both conditions, so an **absent right ureter** fits either one
whyNot.C: The spine forms independently of the metanephros, so a **normal spine** fits either condition
whyNot.D: The heart is normal in both; it says nothing about whether the **left kidney** is present
whyNot.E: A pelvic search for the missing **right kidney** is negative in both conditions, so it does not separate them

answer: An amniotic fluid index of 2 cm
why: With one working kidney the fetus still makes urine and amniotic fluid stays normal. If both kidneys are absent there is no fetal urine, so severe oligohydramnios develops; the fetus lacks the fluid it needs for lung growth and has Potter facies and limb deformities. **Severe oligohydramnios means both kidneys are missing.**

head: Embryologic error
One side or both
Amniotic fluid and lungs
Imaging or exam clue
rows: Incomplete recanalization of the proximal ureter narrows the junction with the renal pelvis
Usually one side (left more often than right); boys more than girls
Amniotic fluid and lungs normal when one kidney is affected
**Dilated renal pelvis and calyces with a normal-caliber ureter and a normal bladder**
Abnormal mucosal folds in the prostatic urethra block urine outflow (boys only)
Both sides: dilated ureters and kidneys on each side
Severe cases: oligohydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia
**Distended, thick-walled bladder with dilated ureters and calyces on both sides**; dilated posterior urethra on voiding cystourethrography
Lower poles of the two kidneys fuse; ascent stops at the inferior mesenteric artery
Both kidneys, joined across the midline by an isthmus
**Lower poles joined in front of the aorta, below the inferior mesenteric artery, with multiple renal arteries**; associated with Turner syndrome
Ureteric bud fails to form or to induce the metanephros on one side
Amniotic fluid and lungs normal (the other kidney makes urine)
**One kidney absent and the other larger than normal (compensatory hypertrophy)**; creatinine usually normal
Same failure of ureteric bud induction, on both sides
**Severe oligohydramnios (no fetal urine) with pulmonary hypoplasia, flat face and limb deformities; fatal**
Both kidneys and ureters absent; bladder small or not seen
Early splitting of the ureteric bud (partial) or a second ureteric bud (complete)

**Two renal pelves or ureters from one kidney**; the upper-pole ureter inserts lower and more medially (Weigert-Meyer rule) and is obstructed or ends in a ureterocele, while the lower-pole ureter refluxes

idea.rule: Severe oligohydramnios with pulmonary hypoplasia = both kidneys absent; normal fluid with a large solitary kidney = one absent.
also: Potter sequence: flat face, limb deformities, pulmonary hypoplasia
Death is from pulmonary hypoplasia, not from kidney failure
Both conditions share the failure of ureteric bud induction

set_title: Normal-gap acidosis from the kidney tubule: which defect
stem: A 20-month-old boy is brought for poor growth, frequent wet diapers and bowed legs. Slit-lamp examination shows crystals in the cornea. Serum studies show hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia and a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, and urinalysis shows glucose and amino acids despite a normal serum glucose.
oneliner: 20-mo M + poor growth + wet diapers + bowed legs + corneal crystals + low K and phosphate + normal-gap acidosis + glucosuria and aminoaciduria → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Distal RTA does not spill glucose and amino acids and does not explain his **corneal crystals**
whyNot.B: Isolated proximal RTA loses only bicarbonate; he also loses **glucose, amino acids and phosphate** and has **corneal crystals**
whyNot.C: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus gives dilute polyuria without acidosis or glucosuria; he has a **normal anion gap acidosis with corneal crystals**
whyNot.E: Type 4 RTA raises potassium; his potassium is **low**

why: Cystine accumulates in lysosomes because the transporter cystinosin is defective. It crystallizes in the cornea and damages the proximal tubule, producing the Fanconi pattern of glucose, amino acid, phosphate and bicarbonate loss, with rickets. **Corneal crystals plus the Fanconi pattern in a young child = cystinosis.**

head: Defect and site
Serum potassium
Urine pH during acidosis
Other urine losses and complications
rows: Alpha-intercalated cells of the collecting duct cannot secrete H+ (H+-ATPase defect, amphotericin B, autoimmune disease)
Hypercalciuria and low urinary citrate: calcium phosphate stones and nephrocalcinosis; rickets or osteomalacia; no glucose or amino acids in the urine
Proximal tubule reabsorbs too little HCO3- (carbonic anhydrase inhibition; the isolated form is rare)
**Below 5.5 once serum bicarbonate has fallen to the lowered threshold**; alkaline if bicarbonate is infused
Bicarbonate wasting; rickets or osteomalacia; no stones; no glucose or amino acids unless Fanconi syndrome is also present
Low aldosterone or aldosterone resistance in the collecting duct lowers K+ and H+ secretion and ammonium excretion
Diabetic nephropathy (hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism), ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, trimethoprim, heparin
Generalized failure of proximal tubule reabsorption
Below 5.5 once serum bicarbonate is low (proximal pattern)
**Glucosuria with a normal serum glucose, phosphaturia, aminoaciduria and bicarbonaturia**; hypophosphatemic rickets or osteomalacia, polyuria
Autosomal recessive defect of the lysosomal cystine transporter (cystinosin, CTNS) damages the proximal tubule
**Corneal cystine crystals on slit-lamp examination**; photophobia, failure to thrive, rickets, kidney failure in childhood

idea.rule: Corneal crystals with proximal tubule wasting in a toddler = cystinosis.
also: Autosomal recessive; CTNS gene encodes the lysosomal cystine transporter
Cysteamine lowers cystine stores
Progresses to kidney failure in childhood

set_title: Cystic kidneys: which inherited or developmental disease
stem: A 26-year-old man has had two episodes of gross hematuria and has hypertension. CT shows multiple cysts in both kidneys.
oneliner: 26M + two episodes of gross hematuria + hypertension + multiple cysts in both kidneys → ?
ask: Which single additional finding would favor tuberous sclerosis complex over autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease?

whyNot.B: Hepatic cysts point toward **autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease**, not tuberous sclerosis
whyNot.C: Berry aneurysms accompany **autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease**, not tuberous sclerosis
whyNot.D: Flank pain with **hematuria** occurs in both conditions
whyNot.E: Both conditions are dominant, so inheritance does not separate them in a patient with **bilateral renal cysts**

why: Tuberous sclerosis (TSC1 or TSC2, which normally restrain mTOR) causes angiomyolipomas, hamartomas of fat, vessels and smooth muscle, that bleed and cause hematuria, alongside renal cysts. Autosomal dominant polycystic disease produces cysts without fat-containing masses. **A fat-containing renal mass means tuberous sclerosis.**

head: Age at presentation
Inheritance and gene
Kidney size and cyst pattern
Outside the kidney
rows: Autosomal dominant; PKD1 (polycystin-1, chromosome 16) in most, PKD2 (chromosome 4) in the rest
**Both kidneys enlarged, cysts in cortex and medulla**
Berry aneurysms, hepatic cysts, mitral valve prolapse; hypertension, hematuria and flank pain
Both kidneys enlarged, with radially arranged elongated collecting-duct cysts
**Congenital hepatic fibrosis with portal hypertension**; Potter sequence with pulmonary hypoplasia in severe cases
Autosomal dominant; TSC1 (hamartin) or TSC2 (tuberin), which normally restrain mTOR
Seizures, ash-leaf macules, facial angiofibromas, shagreen patch, cortical tubers, cardiac rhabdomyomas
**One kidney replaced by non-communicating cysts of varying size with no functioning tissue**; the other kidney is normal (bilateral disease is fatal)
Atretic ureter on the affected side; usually no other organ involved
Nephronophthisis in childhood and adolescence; medullary cystic kidney disease in adults
Nephronophthisis autosomal recessive (nephrocystin, NPHP genes); medullary cystic kidney disease autosomal dominant (UMOD, MUC1)
**Small kidneys with cysts at the corticomedullary junction**
Chronic tubulointerstitial disease: polyuria, anemia, progressive kidney failure; retinitis pigmentosa in some nephronophthisis

idea.rule: Renal cysts plus fat-containing angiomyolipomas = tuberous sclerosis; cysts plus berry aneurysms and liver cysts = autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.
also: Seizures, ash-leaf macules and cortical tubers accompany it
Angiomyolipomas can bleed; mTOR inhibitors shrink them
Cardiac rhabdomyomas appear in infancy

set_title: Vomiting, deep breathing or coma with ketones: diabetic ketoacidosis or a look-alike
stem: A 24-year-old woman has eaten nothing for 5 days and has ketones in her urine. Starvation ketosis and diabetic ketoacidosis are both being considered.
oneliner: 24F + no food for 5 days + ketonuria → Starvation ketosis or DKA?
ask: Which single finding favours starvation ketosis over diabetic ketoacidosis?

options.D: Serum glucose in the normal range
options.E: Fatty acid oxidation in the liver

whyNot.A: Glucagon rises in **both** states and drives fat oxidation, so it does not separate them
whyNot.B: Insulin is **low in both**; only the degree differs
whyNot.C: This is **already in the stem** and occurs in both
whyNot.E: Both states depend on **fat oxidation** for ketone production

answer: Serum glucose in the normal range
why: Both states combine low insulin, high glucagon and fat oxidation that floods the liver with acetyl-CoA, so ketones appear in both. **Starvation leaves the glucose normal or low and the bicarbonate above about 18**, whereas ketoacidosis adds hyperglycemia and a severe acidosis.

pH and bicarbonate
Ketones
Serum osmolality
Typical patient and trigger
rows: Type 1 diabetes with missed insulin or an infection
pH above 7.30 and bicarbonate above 18 mEq/L
Older adult with type 2 diabetes, infection and poor fluid intake
Anion gap acidosis, often mixed with a vomiting alkalosis
Large beta-hydroxybutyrate; nitroprusside test may read weak
**Heavy drinking, then vomiting and days without food**
**Mild: bicarbonate usually above 18 mEq/L, pH near normal**
Insulin or sulfonylurea excess, with sweating and tremor

idea.rule: Ketosis + normal glucose + mild acidosis = starvation; ketosis + high glucose + severe acidosis = DKA.
also: Early in a fast the liver makes glucose from glycogen, then from amino acids and glycerol
The brain switches to ketone bodies after about 3 days
Beta-hydroxybutyrate exceeds acetoacetate in both

set_title: Newborn with ambiguous genitalia, salt wasting or high blood pressure: which steroid enzyme or sex-development error
stem: A 16-year-old girl has primary amenorrhea. Karyotype is 46,XY. She has female external genitalia with a short vagina. Androgen insensitivity syndrome and 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency are both being considered.
oneliner: 16F + primary amenorrhea + 46,XY + female external genitalia, short vagina → Androgen insensitivity or 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency?
ask: Which single finding favours androgen insensitivity syndrome over 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency?

whyNot.A: Testes in **both** make anti-Mullerian hormone, so neither has a uterus
whyNot.B: Undescended **testes** are present in both 46,XY conditions
whyNot.D: Both lack androgen action, so **pubic and axillary hair** is scant in both
whyNot.E: Both have **female external genitalia** and are usually raised as girls

why: Both are 46,XY with testes, female external genitalia and no uterus. In androgen insensitivity the testes make plenty of testosterone, and **aromatization to estradiol gives normal breasts**; in 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency no androgens or estrogens are made, so breasts do not develop and hypertension with low potassium appears.

Blood pressure, sodium and potassium
Precursor that builds up
Cortisol and ACTH
rows: Classic form: low blood pressure, low sodium, high potassium
Cortisol low, ACTH high; renin high
**High blood pressure and low potassium**, low renin
**No sex steroids: 46,XX has no puberty; 46,XY has female external genitalia**
High blood pressure and low potassium, low renin
Cortisol low, ACTH high; androgens and estrogens low
**46,XY with female external genitalia, blind vagina, no uterus and testes**
Testosterone and LH normal to high
46,XX with SRY on an X chromosome: male or ambiguous genitalia, testes

idea.rule: 46,XY female + breasts + normal BP = androgen insensitivity; 46,XY female + no breasts + high BP and low potassium = 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency.
also: Testosterone and LH are normal to high in androgen insensitivity
Remove the testes after puberty because they can become malignant
17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency raises deoxycorticosterone, which lowers renin

set_title: Floppy, jaundiced or very large baby: thyroid, chromosome or a diabetic mother
stem: A 2-month-old girl, born at term weighing 3.1 kg (6 lb 13 oz), is hypotonic and has a protruding tongue and an umbilical hernia. She has upslanting palpebral fissures, a flat facial profile and a single palmar crease.
oneliner: 2F + born at 3.1 kg + hypotonia + protruding tongue + umbilical hernia + upslanting palpebral fissures + flat facial profile + single palmar crease → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: This diagnosis gives a **large** baby with hypoglycemia in the first hours; she weighed **3.1 kg** and is **2 months old** with a typical face and palmar crease
whyNot.B: It shares the hypotonia, tongue and hernia, but it does not cause **upslanting palpebral fissures, a flat facial profile or a single palmar crease**
whyNot.C: Neonatal hypotonia fits, but the **upslanting palpebral fissures, flat facial profile and single palmar crease** are not part of it
whyNot.E: Overgrowth is the rule here, and her birth weight of **3.1 kg** is normal; the **upslanting fissures and palmar crease** do not belong to it

why: Trisomy 21 produces hypotonia, a protruding tongue and umbilical hernia, but also a recognizable face. **Upslanting palpebral fissures, a flat facial profile and a single palmar crease** make the diagnosis; a karyotype confirms it.

stem: A 6-hour-old boy weighs 4.9 kg (10 lb 13 oz) and has a plasma glucose of 22 mg/dL with a high serum insulin concentration. Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and infant of a diabetic mother are both being considered.
oneliner: 6-hour-old M + 4.9 kg + glucose 22 mg/dL + high insulin → Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome or infant of a diabetic mother?
ask: Which single finding favours Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome over infant of a diabetic mother?

why: Both give a big, hypoglycemic, hyperinsulinemic newborn. Only Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome has the **macroglossia and ear lobe creases** of an 11p15 imprinting disorder, and with it comes a risk of Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma.

set_title: No periods by 16 or no puberty: ovary, uterus, androgen receptor or hypothalamus
stem: A 19-year-old woman has never had a menstrual period. Her breasts are Tanner stage 5. Pelvic examination shows a short, blind-ending vagina, and ultrasonography shows no uterus. Pubic and axillary hair are sparse.
oneliner: 19F + primary amenorrhea + Tanner 5 breasts + blind vagina + no uterus + sparse pubic and axillary hair → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Turner syndrome leaves the breasts **undeveloped** and the uterus present; she has **Tanner stage 5 breasts** and **no uterus**
whyNot.C: Constitutional delay ends in normal puberty with a uterus; she has **no uterus** and a **blind-ending vagina**
whyNot.D: Mullerian agenesis gives the same blind vagina and absent uterus but **normal** pubic and axillary hair; hers are **sparse**
whyNot.E: Kallmann syndrome leaves the breasts **undeveloped** with a uterus present; she has **Tanner stage 5 breasts** and **no uterus**

why: 46,XY testes make testosterone that is aromatized to estrogen, so the breasts develop, while a nonfunctioning androgen receptor leaves the body hair sparse. Anti-Mullerian hormone from the testes removed the uterus. **No uterus with sparse pubic and axillary hair** means androgen insensitivity.

Uterus and cervix

set_title: Breast tissue in a boy or man: puberty, a drug, a tumor or a chromosome
stem: A 22-year-old man is evaluated because he and his partner cannot conceive. He is 190 cm tall, with long legs and bilateral breast enlargement. Both testes are small and firm. Serum FSH is high, and he takes no medications.
oneliner: 22M + infertility + 190 cm + long legs + gynecomastia + small firm testes + high FSH + no drugs → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: A testicular tumor presents with a **testicular mass**; his testes are **small and firm** on both sides
whyNot.C: Pseudogynecomastia is fat with **no glandular tissue** and normal testes; he has **small, firm testes** and **high FSH**
whyNot.D: Pubertal gynecomastia occurs in adolescents with **normal** testes; he is **22** with **small firm testes**
whyNot.E: Drug-induced gynecomastia needs a medication; he **takes none**

why: A 47,XXY karyotype causes seminiferous tubule hyalinization, so the testes are small and firm, inhibin falls and **FSH rises**. A tall man with **gynecomastia and small, firm testes** has Klinefelter syndrome.

set_title: Chronic liver test abnormality in an adult: virus, autoimmunity, bile ducts or a metal
stem: A 24-year-old man has fatigue, hepatomegaly and raised aminotransferases. Wilson disease and hereditary hemochromatosis are both being considered.
oneliner: 24M + fatigue + hepatomegaly + raised aminotransferases → Wilson disease or hemochromatosis?
ask: Which single finding favours Wilson disease over hereditary hemochromatosis?

whyNot.B: A high cancer risk belongs to **hemochromatosis with cirrhosis**; the risk is lower in Wilson disease, so it points the other way
whyNot.C: Untreated, **either metal overload** can scar the liver
whyNot.D: Copper in one and iron in the other both **deposit in hepatocytes**
whyNot.E: Both disorders are **autosomal recessive**, so inheritance does not separate them

why: ATP7B mutations block copper excretion into bile and its loading onto ceruloplasmin, so copper builds up in the liver, basal ganglia and cornea. **Low serum ceruloplasmin with high urinary copper** identifies Wilson disease, whereas iron overload shows a high transferrin saturation.

set_title: Odd skeleton from birth: short limbs, missing clavicles, brittle or marble bones
stem: A 3-year-old girl has had four long-bone fractures after minor falls. X-rays show thin, osteopenic bones. Her legs are straight, and her growth plates look normal.
oneliner: 3F + four long-bone fractures after minor falls + thin, osteopenic bones + straight legs, normal growth plates → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Achondroplasia gives short limbs without fractures; she has **four fractures with thin bones**
whyNot.C: Osteopetrosis gives dense bones; hers are **thin and osteopenic**
whyNot.D: Hypophosphatemic rickets bows the legs and widens the growth plates; her **legs are straight and her growth plates look normal**
whyNot.E: Cleidocranial dysplasia leaves bone strength normal; she has **repeated fractures**

why: COL1A1 or COL1A2 mutations (usually autosomal dominant) make too little or abnormal type I collagen, so bones are thin and fracture easily. **Repeated fractures after minor trauma through thin bones** point to osteogenesis imperfecta. Blue sclerae, hearing loss and opalescent teeth often accompany it, and child abuse is the main alternative to exclude.

head: Look of the child
Bone cell or process at fault
Gene and inheritance
Clincher
rows: Short arms and legs, normal-length trunk, large head with prominent forehead and low nasal bridge; normal intelligence
Endochondral ossification: growth-plate chondrocytes fail to proliferate; membranous bone is spared
FGFR3 gain of function; autosomal dominant, usually a new mutation with advanced paternal age
**Short limbs on a normal trunk with normal intelligence**
Absent or hypoplastic clavicles, late-closing fontanelles, extra unerupted teeth
RUNX2 loss of function; autosomal dominant
**Shoulders that meet in front of the chest**
Dense, brittle bones; pallor, infections, enlarged liver and spleen; blindness and deafness from narrowed skull foramina
Osteoclasts cannot acidify and resorb bone; marrow space is lost
Carbonic anhydrase II deficiency (with renal tubular acidosis) or CLCN7; severe forms autosomal recessive, mild adult forms autosomal dominant
**Dense bones with pancytopenia and cranial nerve compression**
Fractures after minor trauma, blue sclerae, hearing loss, opalescent teeth
Osteoblast product: defective type I collagen, so bones are thin
COL1A1 or COL1A2; usually autosomal dominant
**Blue sclerae with fractures and thin bones**

idea.rule: Fractures from minor trauma + thin bones = osteogenesis imperfecta (type I collagen).
also: Blue sclerae: thin collagen lets the choroid show through
Hearing loss and dentinogenesis imperfecta may coexist

set_title: Weak or cramping muscles: a missing protein, a missing enzyme, a potassium shift or disuse
stem: A 4-month-old girl feeds poorly and is floppy. Her tongue is large, and a chest x-ray shows an enlarged heart.
oneliner: 4-month-old girl + poor feeding, floppy + large tongue + enlarged heart on x-ray → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Duchenne muscular dystrophy appears at 2 to 5 years in boys; she is a **4-month-old girl with an enlarged heart**
whyNot.C: Limb-girdle dystrophy begins after infancy; she is a **4-month-old with a large tongue and an enlarged heart**
whyNot.D: McArdle disease causes exercise-induced cramps in teens and adults; she is a **floppy 4-month-old with cardiomegaly**
whyNot.E: Disuse atrophy follows immobilization of a limb; she is **floppy since early infancy with a large tongue**

why: Deficiency of lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase (acid maltase) lets glycogen build up inside the lysosomes of muscle and heart. **A floppy infant with a large tongue and an enlarged heart** is Pompe disease, glycogen storage disease type II. Enzyme replacement therapy is available.

head: Age and inheritance
Pattern of weakness
Key test
Clincher
rows: Boys, usually aged 2 to 5 years; X-linked recessive frameshift deletion of the dystrophin gene
Proximal legs first, then arms; uses hands to push up from the floor
Creatine kinase many times above normal; no dystrophin on muscle immunostaining
**Large, firm, weak calves (pseudohypertrophy) in a young boy**
Teens to adults, either sex; most forms autosomal recessive (for example sarcoglycan genes)
Slowly worsening weakness of the hip and shoulder girdles
Creatine kinase raised; dystrophic biopsy; gene panel confirms the type
**Either sex affected with healthy parents; not an X-linked pattern**
Teens to young adults, either sex; autosomal recessive muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency
Cramps and weakness within minutes of hard exercise; normal strength at rest; dark urine from myoglobin
Venous lactate does not rise after forearm exercise, while ammonia does
**Flat lactate rise with a second wind after a short rest**
Infants in the classic form; autosomal recessive lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase (acid maltase) deficiency
Floppy infant with poor feeding; large tongue; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Low acid alpha-glucosidase activity; glycogen-filled vacuoles in muscle
Teens and twenties, more often male; autosomal dominant calcium or sodium channel gene
Attacks of flaccid weakness of the limbs lasting hours; strength normal between attacks
Serum potassium low during an attack, normal between attacks
**Weakness after a carbohydrate meal or rest following hard exercise, with low potassium**
Any age; follows a cast, bed rest or limb unloading
Wasting and weakness of the immobilized limb only; reflexes and sensation normal
Creatine kinase normal; small fibers without necrosis or inflammation
**Thin limb after immobilization that recovers with exercise**

idea.rule: Floppy infant + large tongue + cardiomegaly = Pompe disease (lysosomal glycogen); exercise cramps with a flat lactate rise = McArdle disease.
also: Autosomal recessive; the only glycogen storage disease that is a lysosomal storage disease

set_title: Shaking, jerking or slowed movements: basal ganglia, cerebellum or copper
stem: A 22-year-old woman has had 1 year of an irregular tremor of both arms, slurred speech, mood swings and falling grades at college. The differential is between Wilson disease and Huntington disease.
oneliner: 22F + 1 year of irregular arm tremor, slurred speech, mood swings and falling grades → Wilson or Huntington?
ask: Which single finding favours Wilson disease over Huntington disease?

options.A: Atrophy of the caudate nucleus on brain MRI
options.B: A father who had the same illness in his forties
options.C: Mood swings and irritability noted by her family
options.D: Golden-brown rings at the corneal edges

whyNot.A: Caudate atrophy is the imaging sign of Huntington disease and favours the other diagnosis
whyNot.B: An affected parent fits autosomal dominant Huntington disease; Wilson disease is **autosomal recessive**
whyNot.C: Mood swings are **already in the stem** and occur in both diseases
whyNot.E: Slurred speech is **already in the stem** and occurs in both diseases

answer: Golden-brown rings at the corneal edges
why: Copper builds up in Descemet membrane of the cornea, in the liver and in the putamen when ATP7B fails to move copper into bile and ceruloplasmin. **Kayser-Fleischer rings** are seen on slit-lamp examination and favour Wilson disease; caudate atrophy and an affected parent mark Huntington disease.

head: Age and family
Kind of movement
When it is worst
Lesion site
rows: Slowness (bradykinesia) with cogwheel rigidity and a pill-rolling tremor
**Tremor at rest that fades with voluntary movement**
Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta; Lewy bodies of alpha-synuclein
Often familial (autosomal dominant); common in older adults
Symmetric tremor of the hands, sometimes the head and voice; no rigidity or slowness
**Absent at rest; appears when the arms are held out or the hands are used; eased by alcohol and propranolol**
Onset at 30 to 50; autosomal dominant, earlier in each generation
Brief, irregular, flowing chorea with dementia and mood change
Constant while awake; worse with stress, gone in sleep
**Atrophy of the caudate and putamen; CAG repeat expansion in HTT on chromosome 4**
Older adult with hypertension or diabetes; sudden onset
Wild, flinging movements of one arm and leg
Continuous while awake, gone in sleep
**Small infarct of the contralateral subthalamic nucleus**
Irregular tremor, dystonia and parkinsonism with psychiatric change
**Copper in the putamen, the cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings) and the liver; low ceruloplasmin**
Any age; stroke, tumor or trauma
Tremor with dysmetria, past-pointing and ataxia on the same side as the lesion
**Absent at rest; grows as the finger nears its target (intention tremor)**

idea.rule: Corneal rings, low ceruloplasmin and liver disease with a movement disorder in a young person = Wilson; dominant family history and caudate atrophy = Huntington.
also: Treat Wilson disease with penicillamine or trientine, or zinc
Wilson disease is autosomal recessive; Huntington disease is autosomal dominant

set_title: Skin marks with brain lesions: which neurocutaneous syndrome
stem: An 11-year-old boy has seven light-brown skin patches and freckling in both armpits. Slit-lamp examination shows small pigmented nodules on the iris.
oneliner: 11M + seven light-brown skin patches + axillary freckling + pigmented iris nodules → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Neurofibromatosis type 2 has few skin patches and bilateral vestibular schwannomas; he has **many brown patches with armpit freckling and iris nodules**
whyNot.B: Tuberous sclerosis causes pale leaf-shaped patches and seizures; his patches are **light brown with armpit freckling**
whyNot.C: Von Hippel-Lindau disease has no skin findings; he has **many brown skin patches**
whyNot.D: Sturge-Weber syndrome causes a red-purple facial stain; he has **brown patches across the body**

why: Neurofibromatosis type 1 results from loss of neurofibromin, a Ras GTPase-activating protein encoded on chromosome 17, and is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait. **Multiple cafe-au-lait spots with axillary freckling and iris Lisch nodules** is NF1.

head: Skin
Brain and eye
Other organs
Gene and inheritance
rows: **Pale ash-leaf macules**, shagreen patch, facial angiofibromas
Cortical tubers and subependymal nodules; seizures and developmental delay
TSC1 (hamartin, chromosome 9) or TSC2 (tuberin, chromosome 16); autosomal dominant; mTOR activation
**Six or more cafe-au-lait spots, axillary freckling**, cutaneous neurofibromas
NF1 (neurofibromin, a Ras inhibitor) on chromosome 17; autosomal dominant
**Port-wine stain in the first trigeminal (V1) distribution**
Leptomeningeal angioma with tram-track calcification; seizures; glaucoma
Somatic GNAQ mutation; sporadic, not inherited
Clear cell renal carcinoma; pheochromocytoma; pancreatic cysts
VHL on chromosome 3p; autosomal dominant; HIF accumulates
**Bilateral vestibular schwannomas**, meningiomas, ependymomas; juvenile cataracts

idea.rule: Cafe-au-lait spots + axillary freckling + Lisch nodules = NF1 (chromosome 17); bilateral vestibular schwannomas = NF2 (chromosome 22).
also: Neurofibromas, optic glioma and pheochromocytoma follow
Lisch nodules are iris hamartomas
Half of cases are new mutations

set_title: Abnormal prenatal screen: which fetal problem gives this pattern
stem: A 39-year-old woman at 12 weeks' gestation has a first-trimester screen. Ultrasound shows increased nuchal translucency, and serum testing shows decreased PAPP-A and increased free beta-hCG.
oneliner: 39F + 12 weeks + increased nuchal translucency + low PAPP-A + high free beta-hCG → ?
ask: Which of the following fetal conditions is most likely?

whyNot.A: Edwards syndrome also gives increased nuchal translucency and low PAPP-A, but hCG is low; hers is **increased**
whyNot.B: An open neural tube defect raises AFP and is not screened by nuchal translucency; she has **increased nuchal translucency with low PAPP-A**
whyNot.C: An abdominal wall defect raises AFP and is seen later on ultrasound; she has **increased nuchal translucency with low PAPP-A**
whyNot.E: Confined placental mosaicism is a villus karyotype finding; she has **a screening pattern of increased nuchal translucency and low PAPP-A**

why: Trisomy 21 raises hCG and lowers PAPP-A, and thickened nuchal translucency adds to the risk. **Increased nuchal translucency with low PAPP-A and high hCG** points to Down syndrome.

hCG
Estriol and inhibin A
First-trimester markers or other test

Estriol low, inhibin A normal or low

Amniotic fluid AFP and acetylcholinesterase high; ultrasound shows a spinal defect
**Ultrasound shows a normal spine and bowel outside the abdominal wall**; amniotic fluid AFP high
**Mosaic trisomy on chorionic villus sampling but a normal karyotype on amniocentesis**

also: Quad screen: low AFP, low estriol, high hCG, high inhibin A

stem: A 36-year-old woman at 17 weeks' gestation has a quad screen. Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein and unconjugated estriol are both low. Serum hCG and inhibin A are both high.
oneliner: 36F + 17 weeks + quad screen with low AFP and estriol and high hCG and inhibin A → ?

whyNot.A: An open neural tube defect raises AFP; hers is **low**
whyNot.B: Edwards syndrome gives low hCG and normal or low inhibin A; hers are **high**
whyNot.C: An abdominal wall defect raises AFP; hers is **low**
whyNot.D: Confined placental mosaicism is found by comparing villus and amniotic karyotypes and does not give this quad pattern; her results are **low AFP and estriol with high hCG and inhibin A**

why: Trisomy 21 gives a characteristic quad screen. **Low AFP and estriol with high hCG and inhibin A** is Down syndrome, and confirmation needs amniocentesis or cell-free DNA.

set_title: Abnormal prenatal screen: which fetal problem gives this pattern
stem: A 41-year-old woman at 18 weeks' gestation has a quad screen with low AFP, low unconjugated estriol, low hCG, and normal inhibin A. Ultrasound shows clenched fists with overlapping fingers.
oneliner: 41F + 18 weeks + low AFP, estriol, and hCG with normal inhibin A + clenched fists with overlapping fingers → ?
ask: Which of the following fetal conditions is most likely?

whyNot.B: Down syndrome gives high hCG and inhibin A; hers are **low hCG and normal inhibin A**
whyNot.C: An open neural tube defect raises AFP; hers is **low**
whyNot.D: Confined placental mosaicism does not cause fetal malformations; she has **clenched fists with overlapping fingers**
whyNot.E: An abdominal wall defect raises AFP with bowel outside the abdomen; hers is **low with clenched fists**

why: Trisomy 18 lowers AFP, estriol, and hCG, and inhibin A stays normal or low. **Low hCG with low AFP and estriol, plus clenched fists with overlapping fingers,** is Edwards syndrome.

set_title: Abnormal prenatal screen: which fetal problem gives this pattern
stem: A 38-year-old woman has chorionic villus sampling at 11 weeks because of advanced maternal age. Villus cells show 47,XY,+16 in 12 of 30 cells and 46,XY in the rest. Amniocentesis at 16 weeks shows 46,XY in all cells examined.
oneliner: 38F + chorionic villus sampling with mosaic 47,XY,+16 + amniocentesis with 46,XY in all cells → ?
ask: Which of the following best explains these results?

options.C: Maternal cell contamination of the culture

whyNot.A: True fetal mosaicism would show the trisomic line in amniotic cells; **all amniocentesis cells are 46,XY**
whyNot.C: Maternal cell contamination adds normal female cells; **every cell here is male and a 47,XY,+16 line is present**
whyNot.D: A sample mix-up gives an unrelated karyotype for the whole sample; here **both normal and trisomic male lines come from one villus sample**
whyNot.E: Pseudomosaicism affects a single cell or colony; here **12 of 30 villus cells carry trisomy 16**

why: A trisomic cell line can arise in the trophoblast after fertilization while the embryo proper stays diploid. **Mosaic trisomy on villus sampling with a normal karyotype on amniocentesis** is confined placental mosaicism.

set_title: Abnormal prenatal screen: which fetal problem gives this pattern
stem: A 35-year-old woman at 17 weeks' gestation has a quad screen with low maternal serum AFP and low unconjugated estriol. A physician is deciding between Down syndrome and Edwards syndrome.
oneliner: 35F + 17 weeks + quad screen with low AFP and low estriol: Down syndrome or Edwards syndrome? → ?
ask: Which additional result best favors Down syndrome over Edwards syndrome?

whyNot.A: Both trisomies lower AFP; **low AFP is already in the stem** and does not separate them
whyNot.B: Both trisomies lower estriol; **low estriol is already in the stem** and does not separate them
whyNot.C: Both are more likely with advancing maternal age; **her age of 35 is in the stem** and does not separate them
whyNot.E: The quad screen is done at 15 to 22 weeks for both; **17 weeks is in the stem** and does not separate them

why: Down and Edwards syndromes both give low AFP and estriol, so those do not separate them. **High hCG** (with high inhibin A) is Down syndrome, whereas low hCG is Edwards syndrome.

set_title: Small testes or low sperm count in a man: steroids, a chromosome, the hypothalamus, a virus or a vein
stem: A 17-year-old boy is tall with long legs and bilateral breast enlargement. He takes no medications or supplements. His testes are small. Serum testosterone is low, and LH and FSH are high.
oneliner: 17M + tall with long legs + gynecomastia + small testes + low testosterone + high LH and FSH → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Mumps orchitis damages the tubules of a testis after puberty and does not change body proportions; he is **tall with long legs and breast enlargement**
whyNot.B: Varicocele gives a left cord mass with normal gonadotropins; his **LH and FSH are high**
whyNot.D: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism gives low LH and FSH; his are **high**
whyNot.E: Anabolic steroids suppress LH and FSH and require androgen use; he **takes no medications or supplements and his LH and FSH are high**

why: A 47,XXY karyotype causes seminiferous tubule dysgenesis and Leydig cell failure, so testosterone falls and LH and FSH rise. **Small testes with high LH and FSH in a tall boy with long legs and gynecomastia** is Klinefelter syndrome.

head: LH and FSH
Serum testosterone
Testes on examination
Other clue
rows: Endogenous testosterone low; sperm count very low
**Muscular man with acne who takes synthetic androgens**
**47,XXY; tall with long legs and gynecomastia**
**No puberty; anosmia in Kallmann syndrome (GnRH neurons fail to migrate)**
FSH high; LH normal or high
**Painful swelling, then atrophy of the affected testis**
Follows parotid swelling; seminiferous tubules damaged
**Left testis smaller; bag-of-worms mass above it that enlarges on standing**
Left side favored because the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein

idea.rule: High LH and FSH with small testes = testis fails (Klinefelter, mumps); low LH and FSH = suppression or hypothalamic defect (steroids, Kallmann).
also: Karyotype 47,XXY from meiotic nondisjunction

set_title: Newborn with calcifications, eye or ear damage, or sepsis after a maternal exposure: which organism
stem: A 5-day-old girl has bilateral white pupils and a continuous machine-like murmur at the left upper sternal border.
oneliner: 5-day-old F + white pupils (cataracts) + continuous machine-like murmur → ?
ask: Which organism is the most likely cause?

whyNot.B: Listeria causes sepsis or meningitis and does not damage the lens or heart; she has **cataracts and a continuous murmur**
whyNot.C: Congenital toxoplasmosis causes chorioretinitis and brain calcifications; she has **white pupils and a continuous murmur**
whyNot.D: Congenital cytomegalovirus infection gives a small head, petechiae and ventricular calcifications; she has **cataracts and a ductal murmur**
whyNot.E: Congenital syphilis causes a runny nose, rash and organomegaly; she has **cataracts and a continuous murmur**

why: Rubella infection in early pregnancy damages the lens, inner ear and heart. **Cataracts with a continuous machine-like murmur from a patent ductus arteriosus** are congenital rubella syndrome; the infection is prevented by vaccinating before pregnancy.

head: Maternal exposure
Brain calcifications
Eyes and ears
Other sign

**Scattered through the brain tissue, with hydrocephalus**
